defaults.permitted_development: Converting an existing residential cellar or basement in England is unlikely to need planning permission where the work stays internal, does not create a separate dwelling and does not materially alter the exterior. New excavation, lightwells or other visible external works can change that answer.

rules.height_rules: There is no separate basement height allowance. The planning issue is usually whether visible guards, railings, lightwell walls or linked above-ground structures become prominent externally.
rules.depth_rules: There is no standalone permitted development depth right for basement excavation. Digging down to create a new basement or materially enlarge one usually needs its own planning assessment, especially where the outside of the property changes.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary-sensitive basement work needs careful review where it introduces lightwells, retaining walls, railings, drainage changes or substantial excavation close to adjoining structures.
rules.roof_rules: If the scheme also includes a rear extension, roof terrace, plant or roof alteration, those elements need their own planning assessment. A purely internal basement conversion does not usually create a separate roof issue.
rules.materials_rules: Visible elements such as front lightwell walls, railings, grilles, doors and paving should be designed as part of the existing house rather than as an awkward add-on. Heritage settings usually need the most restrained detailing.

rules.permitted_development: A straightforward internal basement conversion can often proceed without planning permission, but the position changes if the scheme digs a new basement, forms a separate unit or makes visible external changes such as lightwells, railings or altered entrances.

rules.height_rules: Basement projects are not governed by a simple height cap. The practical question is whether any above-ground parts such as lightwell walls, guard rails, plant or altered entrances materially change the outside appearance.
rules.depth_rules: Depth is often the core basement question, but there is no automatic dig-down allowance. Creating new underground volume, extending beneath the garden or materially enlarging the basement footprint generally needs separate planning review.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary conditions matter most where the basement scheme cuts new lightwells, alters retaining structures or excavates close to neighbouring buildings. Planning, drainage and party wall issues often need to be worked through together.
rules.roof_rules: A basement conversion does not usually create its own roof issue unless the scheme includes associated above-ground work such as terraces, rooflights, plant or linked extensions. Those elements must be assessed separately.
rules.materials_rules: Most material concerns arise only where the scheme changes what you can see from outside. Lightwell linings, guard rails, paving and new joinery should be detailed as part of the host property rather than an obvious add-on.

rules.permitted_development: The easiest basement case is an internal conversion within the existing envelope. Excavation, new lightwells, new self-contained accommodation or other external works are much more likely to need planning permission. This authority also records an Article 4 direction or another local removal of rights, so check the planning history before relying on the simpler route.

rules.height_rules: Height issues arise only when the scheme creates or alters visible above-ground elements. Railings, retaining walls, lightwell upstands and other external additions are usually the parts that need checking.
rules.depth_rules: Basement works do not benefit from a simple excavation allowance. Once the proposal creates new below-ground volume or pushes the basement beyond the existing envelope, expect a distinct planning assessment.
rules.boundary_rules: The planning question is usually hardest at the boundary, especially if the proposal adds lightwells, railings, retaining walls or major excavation next to adjoining property. Structural and neighbour impacts often sit alongside the formal application route.
rules.roof_rules: The roof is rarely the deciding issue for a purely internal basement conversion. It becomes relevant only where the wider project adds external plant, roof alterations or other linked above-ground works.
rules.materials_rules: Where the basement proposal introduces visible external work, keep the materials quiet and well integrated with the house. Front lightwell details, railings and entrance alterations usually need the most careful design.

rules.permitted_development: The easiest basement case is an internal conversion within the existing envelope. Excavation, new lightwells, new self-contained accommodation or other external works are much more likely to need planning permission.

rules.height_rules: Height issues arise only when the scheme creates or alters visible above-ground elements. Railings, retaining walls, lightwell upstands and other external additions are usually the parts that need checking.
rules.depth_rules: Basement works do not benefit from a simple excavation allowance. Once the proposal creates new below-ground volume or pushes the basement beyond the existing envelope, expect a distinct planning assessment.
rules.boundary_rules: The planning question is usually hardest at the boundary, especially if the proposal adds lightwells, railings, retaining walls or major excavation next to adjoining property. Structural and neighbour impacts often sit alongside the formal application route.
rules.roof_rules: The roof is rarely the deciding issue for a purely internal basement conversion. It becomes relevant only where the wider project adds external plant, roof alterations or other linked above-ground works.
rules.materials_rules: Where the basement proposal introduces visible external work, keep the materials quiet and well integrated with the house. Front lightwell details, railings and entrance alterations usually need the most careful design.

rules.permitted_development: Converting an existing cellar or basement is often the lowest-risk route where the work stays internal, does not create a separate dwelling and does not change the outside appearance. A new basement, new lightwell or obvious external alterations will often need planning permission.

rules.height_rules: There is no separate basement height allowance. What matters is whether railings, lightwell upstands, retaining walls, rooflights or linked above-ground works become prominent externally.
rules.depth_rules: There is no standalone permitted development depth right for basement excavation. Digging down to create a new basement, extending below the garden or materially enlarging the underground floorplate usually needs its own planning assessment.
rules.boundary_rules: Basement works near a boundary need close review where they introduce lightwells, retaining walls, drainage changes or excavation close to adjoining structures. In denser areas, party wall and structural issues often run alongside the planning question.
rules.roof_rules: Roof rules usually matter only if the project also includes rooflights, plant, terraces or linked above-ground alterations. A purely internal conversion does not normally create a separate roof issue, but external additions do.
rules.materials_rules: Visible elements such as front lightwell walls, railings, doors, grilles and paving should be designed as part of the existing house rather than as a bolt-on intervention. Heritage settings usually require the most restrained detailing.

rules.permitted_development: A straightforward internal basement conversion can often proceed without planning permission, but the position changes if the scheme digs a new basement, forms a separate unit or makes visible external changes such as lightwells, railings or altered entrances. This authority also records an Article 4 direction or another local removal of rights, so check the planning history before relying on the simpler route.

rules.height_rules: Basement projects are not governed by a simple height cap. The practical question is whether any above-ground parts such as lightwell walls, guard rails, plant or altered entrances materially change the outside appearance.
rules.depth_rules: Depth is often the core basement question, but there is no automatic dig-down allowance. Creating new underground volume, extending beneath the garden or materially enlarging the basement footprint generally needs separate planning review.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary conditions matter most where the basement scheme cuts new lightwells, alters retaining structures or excavates close to neighbouring buildings. Planning, drainage and party wall issues often need to be worked through together.
rules.roof_rules: A basement conversion does not usually create its own roof issue unless the scheme includes associated above-ground work such as terraces, rooflights, plant or linked extensions. Those elements must be assessed separately.
rules.materials_rules: Most material concerns arise only where the scheme changes what you can see from outside. Lightwell linings, guard rails, paving and new joinery should be detailed as part of the host property rather than an obvious add-on.
